Chapter 4. Power, Privilege, and the Art of Reputation
When trouble knocks on the door, some families just huddle together and hope for the best. But the Sacklers? They built themselves a fortress. As the opioid crisis got worse, and OxyContin’s dangers became impossible to ignore, the family didn’t back down—they doubled down, determined to protect their reputation at any cost.
So, what did they do? They brought in top-tier lawyers, world-class PR experts, and a small army of lobbyists who knew exactly how to sway lawmakers and regulators. Their mission was clear: keep the spotlight on their good deeds and make sure no one looked too closely at where their wealth was actually coming from.
Philanthropy turned into their shield. The Sacklers poured millions into museums, universities, and hospitals, making sure their name was on display everywhere—a constant reminder of their supposed generosity. And whenever journalists or activists started connecting the dots between the family and the opioid crisis, the backlash was immediate. Legal threats flew, stories were disputed, and critics were painted as either wrong or out to get them.
Inside the Sackler family, there was this deep sense of entitlement. They firmly believed they’d earned every penny, and that their donations and public works far outweighed any harm that might’ve come from their business. Some family members were hands-on with Purdue Pharma, while others kept some distance—but every single one of them benefited from the fortune OxyContin brought in.
Now, the legal system? It just couldn’t keep pace. Purdue Pharma was hit with lawsuits from states, cities, and people whose lives had been devastated by OxyContin. The company paid out fines and settlements, but the Sacklers themselves? They stayed mostly untouched, their wealth tucked away behind layers of trusts and offshore accounts. Holding them personally responsible turned into a nearly impossible task.
And for a while, this strategy worked. The Sacklers kept their reputation polished, even as evidence against Purdue kept piling up. They still mingled with the elite, showed up at galas, and held prestigious board positions. To most people, they were known as generous philanthropists—not as the masterminds behind a public health disaster.
But you can’t hold back the truth forever. Soon, the cracks began to show. Museums and universities started to wonder if they should keep accepting Sackler money. Activists staged protests, calling for the family to finally be held accountable. And the media? They started digging deeper, pulling back the curtain on connections the family had worked so hard to hide.
Suddenly, it wasn’t so easy to separate the Sackler name from the opioid crisis. That fortress they’d built to protect their legacy? It was beginning to crumble—brick by brick.
